title: Photoelectrons resolve the phase-dependent variance of bright squeezed vacuum
authors: Haoran Ma, Yihe Wang, Chuan Cheng, Ian Gabalski, Aaron M. Ghrist, Eleanor Weckwerth, Mohammed Th. Hassan, Philip H. Bucksbaum
abstract: The variance of bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) is not only strong but also phase dependent, yet recent strong-field experiments with BSV have recorded only its magnitude. A coherent field of the same color provides the phase reference that resolves this phase-dependent noise. Strong-field ionization of xenon by this light shows that the photoelectron yield follows the BSV quadrature along the coherent field, and that the nonlinearity of ionization amplifies the quadrature noise many times over in the electron yield. The noise is moreover distributed unevenly over the photoelectron momentum distribution, differing by an order of magnitude between ionization channels. Strong-field ionization thus offers a phase-sensitive, channel-resolved detector of quantum light, while the quadrature noise of quantum light offers a probe of the intensity dependence of individual ionization pathways.
summary: This paper demonstrates that strong-field ionization of xenon can act as a phase-sensitive detector for bright squeezed vacuum (BSV). By comparing photoelectron noise measurements when the BSV is phase-squeezed versus amplitude-squeezed relative to a coherent field, the authors successfully resolve the phase-dependent variance of the vacuum noise. This technique provides a powerful, non-linear method for characterizing quantum light beyond simple magnitude measurements.
main_problem: The research aims to resolve the phase-dependent variance of bright squeezed vacuum (BSV), a property that has only been measured in terms of magnitude in previous experiments.
main_result: Strong-field ionization of xenon serves as a phase-sensitive detector, showing that the photoelectron yield follows the BSV quadrature, and the measured excess noise decreases predictably when switching between phase-squeezed and amplitude-squeezed light regimes.
method: The study combines quantum optics measurements (using Newton-ring interferometry to characterize the BSV phase) with strong-field atomic physics experiments (ionization of xenon) and theoretical modeling (TDSE calculations).
model_or_system: The physical system is the strong-field ionization of xenon atoms using intense laser light whose vacuum fluctuations are modified by a bright squeezed vacuum state, which is superimposed with a classical coherent field.
key_observables: Field-correlated variance of the photoelectron yield ($	ext{Var}[Y] / \langle N angle^2$), and the measured excess noise ($\Delta g^{(2)}$) as a function of the relative phase ($\phi$).
important_parameters: The relative phase ($\phi$) between the BSV and the coherent field, which dictates whether the measured noise probes the amplitude or phase quadrature of the vacuum.
main_assumptions: The measurement requires careful subtraction of sampling terms to obtain an unbiased estimate of the true variance, and the analysis relies on the assumption that the photoelectron yield is highly sensitive to the BSV quadrature.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the experimental setup involving SHG, PDC, and VMI spectroscopy. Figure 2 compares the measured root-mean-square noise versus the squeezing angle $\phi$ for phase-squeezed vs. amplitude-squeezed light against theory. Figure 3 shows momentum- and energy-resolved photoelectron fluctuations ($\Delta g^{(2)}$) for different light selections.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem (phase-dependent BSV variance), details the experimental setup and methodology (using ionization as a detector), presents quantitative results comparing noise measurements across different phase regimes, and concludes by discussing the implications for quantum light characterization.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum optics (squeezed states) and strong-field physics, demonstrating a novel, highly sensitive, and phase-resolved quantum measurement technique using atomic ionization, which is relevant to advanced quantum sensing.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Experimental arrangement and optical characterization of the BSV field. (a) In the BSV arm, second-harmonic generation (SHG) in a BBO crystal pumps parametric down-conversion (PDC) in two BBO crystals; the 400-nm pump (violet) is then removed by a dichroic mirror. The BSV and the coherent field are combined and focused in the velocity-map imaging (VMI) spectrometer [22–24], which is filled with xenon at low pressure; pick-offs of both arms form Newton rings on a camera, which give the BSV amplitude and phase on every shot (UNWRAP) [25]. Figure 1(b) shows the BSV field distribution measured by the camera. The camera records the amplitude and the phase of each shot, and their joint distribution is the Husimi function of the BSV [30]. The phase jitter between the two arms, about 10◦rms, has been removed from it by deconvolution. The distribution is elongated along one axis, the squeezing axis, with equal populations of the two field signs, and the rms widths of the noisy and quiet quadratures differ by a factor of 6.7 (4.4 before the deconvolution); the quiet width still contains the camera noise, so the ratio is a lower bound.
